findings.title: Unreadable Linux swap inventory suppresses the secret-memory warning
findings.releaseBlockingReason: Low-severity conditional warning omission; this scan is not release acceptance.

reproduction.method: Static source trace, independent baseline challenge and bounded exact-helper Rust probe
reproduction.summary: Synthetic missing and directory-valued `proc/swaps` both yield zero areas, identical to a readable header-only inventory; a visible synthetic swap yields one unknown area. The caller's empty-list branch omits the warning before secret input. FFI, rekey/rehearsal and native protection tests do not establish swap confidentiality.
assertions: Exact probe output: missing_inventory=0 known_empty=0 visible_unknown_swap=1 unreadable_inventory=0.
Current helper source SHA-256 c8ce24394c08c9afedb605b72c2a1c2208a37093cb0f7a42c5b0a2f0a0977bb8; extracted helper SHA-256 b8193f4df970deb1604c762a85266b807b236e28ccadc6a1e507ceac2af6b566.
counterEvidence: Readable ordinary Linux procfs follows the intended detection path.
Small long-lived secret buffers use best-effort mlock; offline/trusted-host guidance remains.
MADV_DONTDUMP and no-core-dump controls address dumps, not swap.
limitations: No real wallet data, full-size Argon2, forced paging, or disk-secret extraction was used.
The probe stubs device resolution only for a positive synthetic control; read-error branches execute the unchanged production helper.

findings.expected: An unreadable swap inventory must be reported as unknown before secrets are read, as SECURITY.md:79–81 promises.
findings.observed: `unprotected_swap_under()` loses the read-error state by returning `Vec::new()`. `settings::warn_about_swap()` interprets an empty vector as no reportable swap and returns. Existing `unknown` flags cover visible areas with unresolved devices, not failure to read the inventory itself. The Argon2 workspace is intentionally not mlocked, so the documented unknown-encryption warning is the relevant residual-risk control.
findings.impact: When Linux denies or omits `/proc/swaps`, secret-handling commands silently skip the swap-encryption warning because an inventory read failure is returned as an empty list. On a host with plaintext swap, this removes the warning before the unlocked Argon2 work area is used; paging and later access to the backing storage are additional prerequisites, not demonstrated secret extraction. The code demonstrably omits a promised diagnostic, but exploitation requires an unusual procfs restriction, active plaintext host swap, actual paging and an adversary with access to its storage. No mnemonic/password input can force that environment, and trusted offline-host guidance remains.
prerequisites: Underlying host uses unencrypted swap, and relevant secret-derived pages actually reach it.
Observer can acquire and read the backing storage.

evidence.label: Swap inventory read collapses failure
evidence.explanation: A Linux procfs read failure becomes an empty list, so callers cannot distinguish unknown inventory from confirmed no swap.

evidence.label: Pre-secret warning gate treats empty as safe
evidence.explanation: The command's pre-secret check receives that empty list and exits silently, suppressing the warning promised for unknown swap encryption.

evidence.label: Argon2 allocation has no page lock
evidence.explanation: The large Argon2 allocation is marked out of core dumps but is not locked against swap; an unreadable inventory is relevant if the host actually pages to plaintext backing storage.

findings.recommendedFix: Represent swap-inventory read failure separately from a confirmed empty inventory and emit an unknown-swap warning before reading secrets; keep existing visible-area classification.
requiredVerification: Missing, denied and unreadable swap inventories must warn as unknown.
A readable header-only inventory must remain a confirmed no-swap case.
Existing plaintext, dm-crypt/LVM and zram tests must retain their outcomes.

confidence.rationale: The exact current helper, extracted unchanged and hash-bound to source, returns zero areas for missing and unreadable synthetic inventories; its caller explicitly returns without warning for zero areas. The independent baseline confirms no alternate inventory warning. Actual host swap leakage was not tested.

findings.title: Generated password can reach the main Windows console when VT activation fails
findings.releaseBlockingReason: Conditional Low privacy failure with a source-supported path and unverified Windows runtime prerequisite; this scan is not release acceptance.

reproduction.method: Independent static source review and adversarial reachability challenge
reproduction.summary: The supported direct invocation is `mhfe encrypt --new-password words --pim 0 --mem 0 --repair-words 0`, followed by a valid 24-word public phrase entered through hidden input. Explicit settings/password/repair options and the 24-word phrase avoid all chooser paths; when Windows VT activation persistently returns false but hidden-input switching succeeds, show writes the password with an inactive guard. This is a source-derived conditional reproduction, not an executed Windows PoC.
assertions: An omitted --repair-words option triggers a chooser whose Windows single_keys refuses failed VT output before password display; this refutes the simpler invocation, not the fully explicit path.
The 24-word original avoids a length chooser; alternatively --same-length explicitly handles a short original.
HiddenInputCheck tests echo-off input only and is full-tier, so startup does not establish private output capability.
counterEvidence: Unix control_sequences returns true; ordinary modern Windows consoles support VT processing.
Generated-wallet phrase display and rekey owner comparison independently check shows_privately and fail closed.
A hostile backup alone cannot force the console API failure, and a trusted host may expose no retained console to another reader.
The original CLI reviewer classified the issue as a robustness gap; the independent challenge retained only the narrow direct path.
limitations: No Windows console host or API failure was reproduced.
No generated secret or real wallet was used; no retained console output was read.
The active screen remains visible by design, so the finding concerns unintended persistence on the main console rather than someone already watching the operation.

findings.expected: Generated secret output must require the actual private screen to be active; terminal-handle preflight alone must not authorize printing after Windows VT activation fails.
findings.observed: can_show_privately checks terminal identity and screen eligibility, while PrivateScreen entry additionally requires control_sequences. A false Windows VT result leaves Flow and PrivateScreen inactive without error. made_password::show then writes the generated secret unconditionally and inactive cleanup never clears that ordinary screen. Refusal gates use the optimistic predicate rather than the acquired privacy state.
findings.impact: An explicitly requested generated container password is printed even if the private-screen guard cannot activate Windows VT processing. With a valid 24-word original and all menu choices supplied, encryption can reach this display using hidden input while leaving the generated password on the ordinary console. A later reader of retained console output could recover that password; actual Windows failure and retention were not reproduced. This is a conditional local privacy failure, not a protocol-input exploit. It requires a console that is recognized as interactive and supports hidden input but repeatedly fails VT-output activation, then a later observer able to read retained console output. Ordinary Windows VT-capable consoles and Unix do not exhibit the challenged condition; practical host occurrence and scrollback recovery remain untested.
prerequisites: Windows standard input/output/error are accepted as the same interactive console; TERM is not dumb.
Windows output VT processing cannot be enabled on each attempt, while input echo-off switching succeeds.
Victim supplies explicit generated-password, PIM, memory and repair-word options and a 24-word original (or explicit --same-length).
Main-console output persists and becomes accessible to the later observer; this condition was not tested.

requiredVerification: Inject a console implementation where terminal identity and hidden input succeed but VT activation returns false; explicit generated-password encryption must refuse before secret output.
